approach.label: How I work
approach.body: I don't hand off sketches and hope. I run the interviews, synthesise the signals, draft the IA, prototype the interactions, then sit beside real users and watch it break. The work only counts when it ships.

2.b: Affinity maps, JTBD, test cards — structured reasoning.

3.b: Figma, Framer, HTML/CSS/React — I build at the fidelity needed.

4.b: Usability test, iterate, hand off with rationale intact.

hero.title: UQ Connect
hero.sub: A social platform for international students, researched and built over one semester.

connect.roleVal: Front-end component system, shared state, 14 of 71 sessions
connect.toolsVal: React · TypeScript · Tailwind · Figma Make · Paper

ch.label: The problem
ch.title: The events already exist. The relationships do not.
ch.p: UQ runs no shortage of events for international students, and students still end up in the same circle. A first-round participant named the ceiling exactly: it is hard to find common ground beyond being international. Large mixers were too loud to hold a conversation in, and event descriptions did not say what would actually happen or what the room would feel like — so a one-off produced an introduction and nothing after it.

re.label: Research
re.title: Three rounds, three fidelities, 71 research and testing records.

m1.b: 33 records in August, 7 of them mine, on why the events that already exist fail to connect people. My seven spanned six countries, seven degrees and three campuses, first year to Master's.

m2.b: 28 records in September, 5 mine, on a prototype that already ran — watching where people stalled.

m3.b: 10 records in November, 2 mine, on the built MVP: one chain, start to finish, unaided. My 14 sessions across the three rounds came from 9 people — 4 sat with me more than once, one all three times.

re.quote: Can I go to the previous page? How can I do that?

sy.label: Synthesis
sy.title: The barrier was pace and group size, not language.
sy.p: Every hypothesis carried a numeric pass mark written before fieldwork began, though we never scored the records against them. Two assumptions did not survive the interviews, on qualitative evidence. Language proficiency was not the barrier — the same students, at the same level of English, went quiet in fast, crowded rooms and spoke freely in small, slow ones. And the gap was not exposure but follow-through: people found the events and still did not go. What did hold was repetition around a shared task — the students who stayed connected had met three or four times over something they were making together, a documentary shoot, a quartet. The cultural society cuts both ways for the same reason: it is the first place a student belongs, and then it is the reason they never leave it.

id.label: Design decisions
id.p: A recommended person shows the reason for the match — shared study habits, compatible schedules — rather than a compatibility score alone. Students were openly sceptical of black-box matching and acted on the same suggestion once it named a concrete reason. The cost is vertical space: fewer matches fit on a screen, and the list takes longer to scan. Discovery moved onto a campus map for a related reason — choosing from a map costs less than choosing from a list — but a map has to say who is already there and whether the walk is safe, or it relocates the hesitation instead of removing it. The competitor teardown pointed the same way: Griffith Mates launches at Orientation, runs a buddy program for four weeks, then keeps people in a Teams channel. The channel is the part doing the work, and a one-off event has no equivalent.

pr.label: Prototype
pr.p: On 3 October, after the September sessions, we stopped patching and redrew the whole application on one sheet of paper: five screens, an arrow for every route off the home page, and one person's name against each feature area. The November build started from that sheet, as a shared component system with React context for cross-screen state rather than nineteen independently styled screens.

te.label: Usability test
te.p: In November a participant completed the full chain unaided — create a circle, set who can see it, open the chat, post, return to the list — and read the colour-coded home screen as a map of the app. The entry point to Circles was still not obvious: he found it in the sidebar rather than on sight.

ou.label: What it produced
ou.p: A 19-screen mobile MVP on a shared component system, reached through three research rounds and a mid-build return to paper — 24 by the team's own MVP definition, which counts sub-views as pages. Evidence status — course project, five-person team. I owned the front-end component system and the shared state layer, wrote some of the backend routes and controllers, and ran 14 of the 71 sessions; the map, the wellness hub and the matching logic were other people's work. In January, after the semester was over, I took the codebase into my own repository and spent five days cutting it back to one design system — plus dark mode, an OAuth callback, and a deploy — across eight commits that added 1,068 lines and removed 2,348. That part is unambiguously mine: nine commits, all under my name, and it is the reason there is a build you can open at all. The MVP runs on mock data: the backend was written and never connected, so matching, messaging and scheduling have never met a real record, a concurrent user, or an empty state. No round recorded completion times or a fixed success criterion, so I can say the September navigation defect did not recur in November, and I cannot say by how much anything improved.

rf.label: Reflection
rf.p: We wrote pass marks and never formally scored them. The thresholds still did real work — they disciplined what we asked, and stopped us reframing misses as findings — but the disconfirmation ended up qualitative, which is the exact failure mode writing them down is meant to prevent. Next time I score the transcripts against the thresholds and publish the table, pass or fail.

hero.title: Spectra Lens
hero.sub: Giving the reader control over type the page author fixed.

ch.label: The problem
ch.title: The page decides how hard it is to read, and the reader has no say.
ch.p: Font, line height, letter spacing and contrast are all set by whoever built the site. A reader who needs looser spacing or a different typeface has no way in. Browser zoom scales everything at once, which breaks layouts and does not touch the typeface at all. Reader modes strip the page down but only work where the site cooperates.

re.label: What I looked at
re.title: Guidelines first, then what already exists.

m1.b: WCAG text-spacing criteria as the starting point for what the controls should cover.

m2.b: How other reading tools handle injection, persistence, and sites that fight back.

m3.b: Why OpenDyslexic exists, what it claims, and what the evidence for it actually is.

re.quote: No user research yet. This case is about what I built and why, not about what it did for anyone.

sy.label: The shape of the problem
sy.title: It has to work on pages that were never built to allow it.
sy.p: Injecting styles into someone else’s page is the whole difficulty. Sites use their own specificity, their own class names, and sometimes inline styles that override anything added later. Anything I inject has to win without breaking layout, and it has to come back the next time that site is opened.

id.label: Design decisions
id.p: The font is bundled in the extension rather than pulled from a CDN: it works offline, it does not tell a third party which pages are being read, and it cannot break when a remote host changes. Settings save per site, because someone who needs looser spacing on a dense documentation page usually does not want it on a news site. The controls sit in a popup rather than a context menu, so the whole set is visible at once instead of hidden behind a right-click.

pr.label: Build
pr.p: A Chrome extension: a content script that injects the style layer, a popup panel holding the controls, a background script keeping settings in sync, and locale files for English and Simplified Chinese. Jest covers the utility layer where the settings logic lives.

te.label: Testing
te.p: Cross-site checks by hand — documentation, news, and single-page apps — to find where injected styles lose to the site’s own CSS. Unit tests cover the settings and utility functions. No participants have used it.

ou.label: What it produced
ou.p: A working extension that rewrites type and spacing on any page from one popup, in two languages, with settings that persist per site. Evidence status — this is a DEMO. It runs, it is tested at the utility level, and it has never been put in front of a reader who needs it.

rf.label: Reflection
rf.p: Building this changed what I think accessibility work is. The guidelines are the easy part; the hard part is that you are a guest on someone else’s page and every site fights you differently. The obvious next step is also the one I have not taken: give it to someone who actually reads this way and watch which controls they never touch.

hero.title: MazeRunners
hero.sub: A physical maze wired so that a ball, a score, a buzz on your finger, and a browser console all describe the same moment.

maze.teamVal: Team project; I owned firmware, sensing, feedback, and the web console
maze.toolsVal: Arduino Mega · Arduino C/C++ · FC-51 IR · TM1637 · Web Serial · JS Canvas

ch.label: The problem
ch.title: A maze is furniture until it answers you.
ch.p: The brief was a physical maze game for a public exhibition. The failure mode showed up in the first build: a nice object that people pushed a ball around while nothing happened. Scoring lived in someone's head, traps were painted lines, and the only feedback was other players laughing. The design problem was not the maze — it was making the system notice events and answer them fast enough that a stranger learns the rules without being told.

re.label: Groundwork
re.title: Working out what the system must sense, and what it must never do.

m1.b: Ten FC-51 IR sensors assigned across trap, diagnostic, spare, and finish zones, each needing its own trigger behaviour.

m2.b: The original trap concept was a mild electric shock. Unsupervised exhibition play made per-person consent and calibration impossible.

m3.b: Score, timer, vibration, lights, audio, and a browser console — each a channel that could carry or muddy the same event.

re.quote: People don't read the score display. They feel the buzz and look up.

sy.label: System concept
sy.title: One event, many channels, one round state machine.
sy.p: Everything hangs off a single round state machine. A ball breaks an IR beam, round state advances, and that one event fans out: score and timer displays update, a vibration pulse fires in the player's finger sleeve, the LED strip and speaker respond, and the browser console logs it. Subsystems reacting independently is exactly what made the first build feel like unrelated gadgets screwed to plywood.

id.label: Technical decisions
id.p: Vibration replaced the electric shock: relay-driven motors in wearable finger sleeves keep the sensation on the body without a risk that needs supervision. Each IR sensor got debounce and a cooldown window, because raw reads double- and triple-fired on a single pass and broke agreement between score, timer, and haptics. Platform tilt moved to its own SafeTouchServoController with hold-to-move behaviour, so servo motion stopped competing with time-sensitive sensor polling and a servo fault could not take down the round.

pr.label: The web console
pr.p: A browser-based system console connects over Web Serial and mirrors the maze live: score and timer HUD, hardware bay, event log, and feedback simulation on a canvas. It also runs standalone in demo mode, because the hardware is not in the room during development — or in a portfolio, or an interview. Regression tests cover serial sync, feedback sync, servo response, and audio parity so the demo cannot quietly drift away from what the firmware does.

te.label: Testing and iteration
te.p: Bench testing tuned debounce and cooldown until one ball pass produced exactly one game event. Parity tests caught drift whenever the firmware or the console was edited alone. Group play at the exhibition then surfaced what the bench could not: players reacted to vibration and audio faster than to the score display, and the finger sleeves had to be fitted for people rather than self-fitted — the setup ritual turned out to be part of the interaction.

ou.label: What it produced
ou.p: A working, exhibited system: firmware modules for game state, IR sensing, player chain input, vibration and audio; a two-controller hardware split; and a browser console with parity tests. Evidence status — this is a university project built for one exhibition. Play was observed, not instrumented, so I can describe what players reacted to but cannot quantify which channel carried the most information.

rf.label: Reflection
rf.p: The strongest lesson was that on hardware, timing is design. Debounce sounds like an electronics detail until a double-fire makes the score disagree with the buzz on your finger, and the player stops trusting the system. The weakest part is that I proved the loop works without measuring which parts of it mattered — rebuilding it, I would log every sensor event and feedback fire from day one, then start switching channels off to find out which ones players were actually using.

hero.title: Vigil
hero.sub: An email review desk built to find out whether an interface can keep someone checking an AI that is wrong 12% of the time.

vigil.roleVal: Designer and technical director; Claude Code and Codex wrote the code to my spec
vigil.timeVal: 2026 · abandoned 23 Sep 2026; evaluation protocol written, study never run
vigil.teamVal: Solo, working through an AI coding workflow; brief sourced from a UQ research lab
vigil.toolsVal: React · TypeScript · Zustand · Dexie · Python · Claude Code · Codex

ch.label: The problem
ch.title: Oversight is the easiest thing in the world to fake.
ch.p: The brief was to design interfaces that help a person oversee an AI screening email for phishing. The trap is in that sentence. Give someone a queue, a verdict and a confidence score, and they will clear it — quickly, agreeably, and without reading much. Throughput looks fine. The interface looks like it worked. What actually has to be designed is not a review screen but the conditions under which reviewing happens at all, and those conditions live in details as small as whether a number is rendered as 0.91 or as HIGH.

re.label: Groundwork
re.title: Before designing the interface, I had to build something worth reviewing.

m1.b: Public phishing corpora are 2002–2015 mail, carry real personal data, and cannot guarantee the character offsets that cue highlighting needs. I wrote 140 messages inside a fictional company instead.

m2.b: No model — a scripted classifier at 87.9%, with its 17 errors placed deliberately: false positives cluster in marketing mail, false negatives in social-engineering messages that carry no links to flag.

m3.b: In the first build every correct call sat at 0.84 or above and every error at 0.82 or below. A reviewer could have caught all seventeen errors by reading a number instead of an email.

re.quoteWho: The classifier panel, when your call and its call disagree

sy.label: System concept
sy.title: Useful and unreliable at the same time — and provably so.
sy.p: Everything hangs on one property: the classifier has to be genuinely helpful and genuinely untrustworthy at once. Confidence is stratified so it ranks the classifier's own errors barely better than chance — an AUC of 0.72 — and the build script refuses to write the corpus if that ever climbs past 0.75. Seven errors carry high confidence; thirty-six correct calls carry low confidence. Someone reading only the number cannot shortcut to the answer, which is the single condition under which comparing two interfaces measures anything at all.

id.label: Design decisions
id.p: Three questions, six variants, all switchable at runtime. How confidence is shown: a precise figure, or a three-step band. When the verdict appears: on open, or only after the reviewer commits to their own call. How evidence is presented: highlighted in the message, or listed beside it. Each variant carries a written argument and a written risk, and my predicted winner for each is on record, dated before I flipped a single one. The interface also refuses things a real security console has — no search, no batch actions, no severity tiers, no reassuring green anywhere. Every one of them would help an operator and blur the measurement.

pr.label: How it got built
pr.p: I did not write the code. Claude Code and Codex built the corpus pipeline, the single-file prototype and the React implementation from a frozen spec, and they were fast — six variants exist because building the sixth cost hours instead of weeks. What did not delegate was the judgement. The first visual pass came back competent and generic: white cards on grey, a safe blue accent, six letterspaced labels on one screen. It looked like software rather than like a decision, and rejecting it is where the interface actually started. The same applies to a generated explanation that described cues the email did not contain — the tooling produced it fluently, and only reading the output against its own data caught it.

te.label: Testing and iteration
te.p: Not yet run with people, and this case says so plainly. The protocol is written: fifteen minutes each, five participants on a rotating variant assignment so every variant gets watched at least twice, with the observation list drawn from the three open questions rather than from a generic script. What holds the build together in the meantime is machine checking — 176 assertions across all eight variant combinations, 101 unit tests over the same decision and scoring rules in the React build, and a palette whose text contrast is measured with a script rather than eyeballed — one token failed at 4.41 and was reworked before it shipped.

ou.label: What it produced

m1.label: confidence as a predictor of the AI's errors

ou.p: A running system with the study still ahead of it: a validated corpus, six switchable interfaces, a React build with durable logging and CSV export, and a test protocol ready to run. Evidence status — nobody outside the project has used it. Everything here is design reasoning and machine verification, not user evidence. The three design questions are open, my predictions are recorded, and the gap between those predictions and the result is the next thing this case will contain.

rf.label: Reflection
rf.p: What surprised me is where the failure mode of an AI-assisted workflow actually sits. It is not bugs — the code was fine. It is that everything the workflow produces is plausible: a competent visual pass, a fluent explanation for an email, a reasonable-looking spread of confidence values. Plausible is exactly what you cannot catch by reading quickly. The three decisions I am proudest of here are all rejections, and all three came from checking generated output against its own data rather than against my taste. The weakest part is the obvious one: I have designed the conditions for a study worth running, and have not yet run it.

hero.title: Hoop Dream
hero.sub: A career simulation that runs from a neighbourhood court at twelve through to retirement — and the production pipeline that wrote down what the world looks like before the asset batches.

hoop.roleVal: Designer, art director and technical director, through an AI production pipeline
hoop.toolsVal: Phaser · TypeScript · Vite · Tailwind · Vitest · Claude Code · Codex

ch.label: The problem
ch.title: Generating the art is cheap. Making it agree is not.
ch.p: A career-simulation RPG needs hundreds of assets — portraits, scenes, story CGs, UI icons, court diagrams — before it reads as one world rather than a folder of pictures. Generation removed the cost of producing them and left the harder problem completely intact: every image can pass the rules on its own, and what is wrong with the set only shows once they sit on the same screen, by which point there are 299 specs on the registry to reconcile.

re.label: Groundwork
re.title: Deciding what the world is, and what it is not.

m1.b: Three reference documents — pixel players, organic scenes, flat logos — split by canvas size and written before the asset batches. Their forbidden lists went into the prompt templates as negative prompts.

m2.b: NBA 2K MyCareer for the career arc, Punch Club for attribute decay, New Star Soccer for life outside the game, Stardew Valley for daily-loop satisfaction. Naming what to borrow from each kept the scope from becoming 'a basketball game'.

m3.b: Photoreal, 3D, anime, neon, random text, real trademarks. Written down as out of bounds, because a generator produces all of them happily on a slightly different prompt.

re.quote: Avoid photo realism and dramatic cinematic lighting.

sy.label: System concept
sy.title: What a script can check, and what only a person can.
sy.p: The rules sit in two places: the art bible, and the prompt templates that carry its forbidden lists as negative prompts. A registry then logs each batch — 64 portraits, 40 scenes, 73 CGs, 72 UI icons, 18 court and tactics, 32 static VFX. A script checks that registry: names, unique keys, folders and, where a file exists, the PNG size read from its header. It cannot see style, so style review stayed manual, with the assets laid side by side against the art bible. The production log's own review line is printed by the generator script, so I do not count it as a review. The images behind the 299 registered specs are not yet verified.

id.label: Design decisions
id.p: A career from twelve to retirement runs on 146 discrete nodes in eight kinds — training, match, story, relationship, risk, reward, rest, legacy — rather than a simulated calendar, because calendar-based career sims spend most of their runtime on repetition and bury the interesting decisions in maintenance clicking. Action combinations carry consequences instead of just numbers: repeated training raises readiness while raising body risk and pressure and lowering team trust. The visual language is reverse-engineered from Anthropic's product design — warm parchment, terracotta accent, exclusively warm-toned neutrals — because a game about one person's whole life needed a surface that reads as unhurried rather than as a sports UI of cold blues. That derivation is stated in the design document; it is a transfer exercise, not an invention.

pr.label: How it got built
pr.p: Claude Code and Codex wrote the implementation against a spec that was frozen first, which is what made the volume survivable — draft, contracts, seasons, off-season, retirement, New Game+ and tactical matches all landed as systems rather than as scripted scenes. Save data carries a schema version, so an old save is migrated rather than silently broken when a chapter lands. The discipline that mattered was not speed but sequencing: rules before output, every time.

te.label: Testing and iteration
te.p: 355 test files and 1,975 tests cover the career, contract, injury, season and save systems. At this size that is a design constraint rather than a boast — without it, adding a chapter quietly breaks a contract rule three chapters earlier, and you find out from a player instead of from CI. The art pipeline went through its own iteration. Every logo passed the per-image rules, yet laid side by side they were variants of one template. That added two set-level rules to the logo bible and to its template's negative prompt: no shared shield-and-big-letters template, and no basketball seams on every logo.

ou.label: What it produced

m1.label: asset specs registered across six batches

ou.p: A publicly playable ten-chapter career sim, built on a pipeline whose style rules are written down rather than kept in my head. Evidence status — the game labels itself DEMO v0.6, and there has been no player research. Everything here is systems design and production discipline; whether the pacing works for someone who is not me is untested. The first load is also large and mobile QA is thin, which matters because a phone is where this audience would meet it.

rf.label: Reflection
rf.p: The useful discovery was that the rejected list did more work than the positive description. 'Warm, simplified, flat symbolic UI' is an opinion two people can hold and still disagree about a specific image. 'Not photoreal, not 3D, not anime, not neon, no random text, no real trademarks' is a test — you can hand it to someone else and get the same answer. When production volume goes up, the rules that survive are the ones that can be checked without you in the room. They are still checked by a person, by eye: the only automated check in the pipeline reads the manifest, and the part a script can automate turned out to be exactly the part that is not style.

hero.title: PriceWise
hero.sub: A grocery comparison prototype across three Australian chains, running on demo data — and the four classes of defect that a passing build, a clean type-check and a green test suite could not see.

pricewise.roleVal: Product direction, interaction design and technical direction; Codex and Claude Code wrote the implementation
pricewise.toolsVal: Next.js · Prisma · Clerk · Postgres · Vitest · Playwright · Codex · Claude Code

ch.label: The problem
ch.title: When an AI writes the code, a green build stops being evidence.
ch.p: The interface rendered. The type-check was clean. 307 unit tests passed. None of those three facts tells you whether a feature actually executes — and in this codebase, four classes of defect satisfied all three. That is the real problem this case is about: not what to build, but how to confirm what was built is real.

re.label: How they were found
re.title: Stop reading the code. Call the endpoint and read what comes back.

m1.b: Semantic search never used a vector — the product object dropped its vector field at the data-mapping layer and every query silently fell back to keyword matching. Keyword matching returns results too, so nothing looked wrong.

m2.b: Lists built from a template were always empty: the items the front end sent were silently stripped by back-end validation. The catch branch also showed a success message, so a dropped network still reported good news.

m3.b: Six declared tables had never been created. Nothing read or wrote them, so 'relation does not exist' had never been triggered. Reading code during a migration also turned up cron auth that did not fail closed when its key was unset.

re.quote: They all pass build, type-check and tests. What is broken is whether the feature runs at all, and no automatic gate is watching for that.
re.quoteWho: The property all four classes share

sy.label: The system idea
sy.title: 'Renders correctly' and 'executes correctly' are different claims.
sy.p: Only one of them has automatic gates behind it. A build proves the code compiles; a test proves the path the test walks; a screenshot proves pixels. None of them proves that a query used the index it was supposed to, that a write landed, or that a declared table exists. The verification pass in this project is simply the habit of asking the second question out loud, on every feature, with the deployed system rather than the source.

id.label: The decision I am least comfortable with
id.p: One more defect was mine: a regression from my own fix to search. Passing a missing field through serialized a 1,536-dimension vector into the API response and pushed three search results to 89 KB. I found it by calling the real endpoint and reading the response, not by reviewing my own diff. It stays in the case because a check that only catches the AI is not really a check. It also shows the method's limit: nothing prevented the defect, something caught it afterwards.

pr.label: How the scope grew
pr.p: The feature list was AI-generated planning, derived from what a complete product ought to have rather than from anyone's need. Phases 2 through 6 all landed across two days, 9–10 January 2026. On 1 March a single commit added 5,884 lines: a v1 API, AI function calling, bilingual text, price prediction, and a social layer of friends, DMs, feeds, household groups and challenges that made up about a quarter of it. On 2 March I stopped, and did not touch it for five months. The scope never came back down: in August the v1 routes moved to unversioned paths rather than being removed, and the social routes are still in the app. Looking back, a comparison app on simulated data with no registered users should not have kept growing.

te.label: The module everything depends on
te.p: Receipt matching is the product: a receipt prints MLK FC 2L, the catalogue says Full Cream Milk 2L, and if those do not meet, nothing else can happen. That module was written in one pass of 175 lines in the second commit and never modified, with 13 tests using 'milk', 'eggs', 'sourdough bread' — not one input resembling printed receipt text. Against 20 constructed receipt-format inputs it matched 15; after a fix that only adds points and never subtracts, 19. All 15 originally-correct inputs held. 311 tests green.

ou.label: What this case produced

m1.label: classes of defect passing build, types and tests

ou.p: A deployed comparison prototype on demo data, covering Coles, Woolworths and Aldi across 65 products — and, more usefully, a verification habit with scripts anyone can re-run. Evidence status: zero registered users. Every verification ran on data I created, and what a real crumpled receipt does to recognition accuracy is unknown to me. The verification is also manual: it should be a build gate, and it is not one yet.

rf.label: Reflection
rf.p: One mismatch was left unfixed on purpose. 'MLK FC 2L' moved from no-match to matching Oat Milk — a change in kind, and for the worse. A no-match lands in the unmatched list where the user can see it; a wrong match sends a wrong price silently into the comparison and the user never finds out. Fixing it means either an abbreviation dictionary, which becomes an endless maintenance list, or admitting two-letter tokens, which reinstates the mis-matches just suppressed. The correct handling is to send it back to no-match, which is a confidence-threshold problem rather than an abbreviation problem. It is pinned by a test so that if it changes, someone knows.

hero.title: Perception Gap Mapper
hero.sub: I built the first working prototype, then argued for abandoning it. The better it looked, the more visible a promise it could not keep.

gapmapper.roleVal: Team project; I built the first prototype and drove the change of direction
gapmapper.timeVal: 2026 · DECO7380 Design Computing Studio 3, submitted and marked
gapmapper.toolsVal: Semi-structured interviews · thematic coding · Figma · literature review

ch.label: The problem
ch.title: A system that recommends a safer route claims an authority it has not earned.
ch.p: The team had nothing demonstrable and I was the one who could turn discussion into code, so the first route-support prototype was mine. It ranked the same trip by different cues, with layers for risk density, lighting, surveillance and open businesses. It looked extremely usable — which is exactly what made it dangerous. It made an unsolved problem look solved.

re.label: Research
re.title: Three people differed on whether to trust a tool.

m1.b: Visibility, main roads, transit stops, bike coverage, streetlights, businesses still open, location sharing, live foot traffic. All three mentioned lighting. In the team's coding chart, people presence came up in 16 of the 18 interviews and lighting in 14: counts of mentions, not a rate.

m2.b: Crime history. One participant was wary of routing by it because bias can already be inside the data before an algorithm touches it — and because a conclusion you cannot interrogate is not usable. I mis-read her point at first and went back to the notes after a teammate challenged me.

m3.b: I had treated streetlights as a directly usable safety variable: more light, safer. Literature disagreed. Visibility, enclosure, nearby activity, social cues and time all change how one light is read. A lit street that is empty, enclosed and hard to leave still feels wrong.

re.quoteWho: The team name, from a week-three exercise: ask what the worst version would do. After critique I realised those four descriptions were our own version.

sy.label: The core structure
sy.title: Two kinds of evidence, side by side, never merged.
sy.p: Objective indicators — lighting, transit access, incident context, sightlines, open businesses, street condition — sit next to perception signals: someone crossing to avoid one side, looking for a shop still open, checking help is close enough, feeling uncertain in a place that is entirely normal on paper. The gap between them is displayed as a reason to investigate, not as proof of danger. Merge them into one score and the uncertainty disappears; the screen starts looking more confident than it has any right to be.

id.label: The turn
id.p: After critique the first thing I changed was not a screen — it was the reader. From a pedestrian who is nervous right now, to councils, city planners and campus safety teams. Output changed with it: no longer telling anyone which way to walk, but showing where perception and objective indicators fail to agree. And the claim changed: it can support a discussion about what to investigate next, and it promises that nowhere is safe. Critique had named two design problems rather than feature gaps — painting safety as binary, and a women's-safety project that risks once again asking women to change their behaviour instead of questioning the environment.

pr.label: The screen that carries it
pr.p: Place Inspector is the load-bearing one. Selecting a place does not return a colour block or a warning: it shows confidence level, source status, report context, and what the data still cannot prove. A red or orange marker on a real street starts to read as a verdict even when the evidence behind it is thin. I ran four questions over every screen — what does this make visible, what does it hide, who does it expect to act, how much certainty does it imply. The map is only the entry point; the argument lives in the slow screens: Place Inspector, Field Reports, Data Sources, Intervention Planner, Ethics Boundary, Export Brief.

te.label: Three interlocking deliverables
te.p: The final report sets the claim: move from route advice to the perception gap, because formal indicators and lived experience do not always agree — a street can be lit, well served by transit and low on recorded incidents, and still be unpleasant to walk. The one-page brief turns the claim into system requirements: reports anonymous, location rounded to a street segment, confidence level and bias notes displayed, no public safety score. The prototype turns those requirements into a flow that runs end to end. The brief was the hardest to write, because it stops an ethical position from being a sentence in a report.

ou.label: What this case produced

m1.label: interviews across the team; three are mine

m2.label: deliverables that hold each other up

ou.p: A design direction that can be challenged: anonymous perception reports, objective layers, gap categories, per-place explanation, source limits, an exportable planning brief. A reviewer, planner or community member can point at a screen and question its logic — which is more useful than a handsome dashboard image. Evidence status: never tested with real planning staff, and parts of the data layer are an intended integration rather than a live pipeline. 18 interviews can count mentions; they cannot support a rate, a ranking or a score, which is why they are used as perception cues throughout.

rf.label: Reflection
rf.p: The main lesson was not 'collect more data'. It was to work out what the data is allowed to claim. Australia already has established channels for residents to report local issues to council; we borrowed the flow but not the purpose — a perception report should not become a public danger warning, only a small planning signal to be checked against other evidence. Community-contributed geographic data can show planners what official layers miss, but it is not automatically complete, neutral or representative, which is why rounding, anonymity and bias notes are preconditions rather than features. I do not think the final proposal fully answers the critique it responded to. It changed what I am willing to claim: not 'help someone walk home safely', but 'help an institution see where its own evidence is incomplete'.

hero.title: Requirements into Rules
hero.sub: Two briefs from one course, doing the same thing: taking a requirement everyone agrees with and forcing it into a rule that can be built to — and argued against.

rules.roleVal: Fietspad was a team project and I was Lead Developer: I built the back-end prototype with AI coding tools and generated the high-fidelity interface in Figma Make, which a teammate rebuilt in Figma Design; the Quest 3 guide was individual and entirely mine
rules.timeVal: 2025 · DECO7250 Human-Computer Interaction, submitted and marked
rules.toolsVal: Figma · Figma Make · Miro · Otter · ChatGPT · literature translation

ch.label: The problem
ch.title: 'Make cycling safer' is a sentence nobody can build to and nobody can argue with.
ch.p: Neither can 'warn people in time'. Everyone agrees with them in a document, and neither survives contact with an engineer. The real design work happens in the step that forces them into numbers: how many metres before the hazard, which lane types get down-weighted, how small a tap target may be, and when not to warn at all. Once that is done the rule can be executed — and, more importantly, someone can point at it and say this one is wrong. Being refutable is the precondition for being useful.

re.label: Working with AI
re.title: AI is an accelerator for breadth. Depth is still a person's job.

m1.b: Generative drafts produced claims that sounded settled and had nothing behind them. Every figure without a source was deleted, claims were verified against official sources, and known local examples went in instead.

m2.b: Figma Make's layout fidelity was unstable — a small prompt change caused a large deviation. It was demoted to a reference export, and every screen was rebuilt in Figma Design.

m3.b: AI merges contradictory findings into a single theme. Edge cases went into a separate table — night-riding confidence, wet-weather risk, large e-bikes that do not fit narrow racks — and each later became a specific feature.

re.quote: Verify transcripts against audio · check claims against official sources · rewrite AI copy · walk the flow with think-aloud · delete features that only add complexity
re.quoteWho: Quality control, as five actions rather than an attitude

sy.label: The system idea
sy.title: The proposal drafts turned safety into metres, pixels and routing weights.
sy.p: Bike lanes end abruptly and dump riders into traffic. The proposal drafts named the phenomenon, the '25-metre bike lane', and proposed down-weighting lanes that are only a layer of paint; AI wrote most of those drafts. The back-end prototype I built with AI coding tools filters segments by level of traffic stress, and the final proposal made 'Calmest' the default route. Hazard categories are cycling-specific rather than generic: left hook, dooring zone, shared lane. The drafts set warnings 150–250 m ahead, delivered by audio and haptics so they do not take the eyes, and a 48 px tap-target floor is one item on the drafts' self-check list. The final proposal kept pre-alerts before roundabouts and left hooks.

id.label: Interface decisions
id.p: Warnings state behaviour, not direction: take the lane and make eye contact with turning drivers, or take the alternate street — because that is the real response to a left hook, not 'turn left'. The detour button carries its own cost, stating the extra minutes on the button itself, while 'keep current route' remains an equal-weight primary action; the interface does not assume the safer route is the right route. Distances are given as distance — 200 m, 450 m, 1.2 km — not as junction counts, because there is no stable 'next intersection' while riding. And the entry button reads 'See safer routes', comparative rather than superlative, because no available data supports the word 'safest'.

pr.label: The second brief
pr.p: A VR headset watches your hands with cameras. In low light, when the hands overlap, or when a hand leaves the field of view, tracking breaks and the virtual hand vanishes. A 2025 peer-reviewed paper showed that warning before the break is effective. The brief was to turn that into something a designer can act on tomorrow: three failure causes became three independent trigger conditions with their own copy, rather than one generic warning; the detection lead time became a per-cause threshold — roughly three seconds ahead in low light, risk-threshold triggers for out-of-view and occlusion, ignoring micro-jitter and applying a cooldown; and the copy convention became uniform, symptom then one action, verb first.

te.label: How far the testing went
te.p: Think-aloud walkthrough, and no further. The proposal drafts' self-check list claims 6 of 6 — which is a self-check, not external validation, and the case says so rather than letting the number imply more. A walkthrough catches comprehension problems. It does not catch what happens when someone is riding, tired, wet or in traffic, and the audio warning in particular exists precisely because a rider cannot look at a screen.

ou.label: What this case produced

m1.label: warning lead in the proposal drafts

m2.label: tap-target floor, one item on the drafts' checklist

ou.p: A route app's interface and design system, an AI usage register, an eight-panel guide and its analysis. Evidence status: both were submitted and marked, neither shipped. The guide's effect figures — roughly 83% for out-of-view and 62% for mutual occlusion — are the cited paper's experimental results, not mine, and a separate section lists what that study cannot support: three causes only, Quest 3 only, mostly right-handed young participants, short lab tasks. Fietspad's route proportions are demonstration figures.

rf.label: Reflection
rf.p: Putting the two briefs together is the point. In Fietspad, the proposal drafts turned 'safety' into routing weights, warning distances and tap sizes, and AI wrote most of those drafts. The other brief is where I turned a paper into trigger conditions, copy templates and a checklist myself. What survives outside a course is the move itself — and the discipline of saying where the rule stops holding, rather than letting a self-check stand in for evidence someone else produced.
